name: L-theanine
summary: L-theanine is an amino acid found mainly in tea. It is sold as a supplement for relaxation, sleep and focus.
commonUses: May reduce stress and anxiety in people under stress.
May improve focus and attention, alone or together with caffeine.
roles: L-theanine is not an essential nutrient. It may act on brain messengers, but human evidence is small, often short and mixed.

status.note: This basic guide does not provide a routine status test.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

forms.name: Plain L-theanine capsules or tablets
forms.note: Most trials of one ingredient used about 200 to 400 mg.

forms.name: Theanine with caffeine
forms.note: Common in studies of focus; effects were measured mostly within about two hours.

forms.name: Magnesium L-theanate or blends
forms.note: Mixed products; results cannot be credited to theanine alone.

reference.noUpperLimit: No tolerable upper intake level for L-theanine was found in the searches of Europe PMC and the reviews read. Absence of a limit does not mean that large amounts have been shown to be safe.

interactions.note: Small studies suggest theanine may blunt blood pressure rises under stress; combined effects with blood pressure medicines have not been properly studied.

interactions.with: Sedatives and sleep or anxiety medicines
interactions.note: Theanine has been compared with a sedative in one anxiety study; combining them has not been well studied, so added drowsiness cannot be ruled out.
In one trial theanine reduced caffeine's rise in blood pressure; mood and focus results for the pair are modest and mixed.

cautions: Reported side effects in trials are mostly mild (headache or drowsiness in some people), but long-term safety data are limited.
Pregnancy, breastfeeding and children: not enough safety data were reviewed, so a doctor should be asked first.
People taking blood pressure, sedative or psychiatric medicines should ask a doctor or pharmacist before adding it.
Persistent anxiety or sleep problems need a doctor's assessment, not only a supplement.

origin: L-theanine is an amino acid (a building-block-like molecule) found almost only in tea leaves (Camellia sinensis) and in a few mushrooms. It is chemically close to glutamate, a brain messenger, and it can cross into the brain. Shade-grown teas such as matcha are often described as richer in it, but this was not checked in a source read for this entry.

Supplements usually contain L-theanine made by fermentation or chemical synthesis, sold as capsules, tablets or drinks, sometimes mixed with caffeine, magnesium or other ingredients. Trial results for mixtures cannot be credited to theanine alone.
dosage: No reference intake or tolerable upper intake level for L-theanine was found from EFSA or other official sources in the searches made for this guide. Tea drinks contain only small amounts of theanine.

An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is about 100 to 400 mg a day (single doses of 200 to 250 mg and daily amounts of 200 to 400 mg appear in the trials reviewed). This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

When reading a label, check how much pure L-theanine one serving holds. Some products use branded forms or blends with caffeine, magnesium or herbs, so the amount per capsule may differ from the amount per daily serving.

foodAmounts.verdict: Partly. Theanine is found in tea leaves, mostly green tea, but amounts vary widely with the tea and how it is brewed, and this guide has no checked per-food figures, so it cannot say how many cups match 100 to 400 mg.
foodAmounts.notChecked: Theanine is not measured in the UK food table used by this app, so no per-food amounts are listed.
